summary:
Borno stands under the national framework of Nigeria, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests on Borno's own legislation as well as that framework. The state's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000) was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act and pimping offences in the state. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender' shall upon conviction be punished with death. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. The death penalty for same-sex intercourse is enacted in Borno's own statute, so the state's criminalisation does not depend on the federal framework for its severity.

Borno is among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, according to Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. Borno enacted a separate Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003. The parallel Shari'a layer in Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

The Shari'a provisions that apply to Muslims in Borno, as one of the twelve northern states, criminalise same-sex sexual acts between men and between women. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria (June 2025) records the maximum penalty for sodomy for men as death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note devotes a section to enforcement of the Shari'a provisions and the posture of the hisbah morality police.

Exposure differs by religion and by court. Shari'a courts hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law, while the 2000 state statute assigns cases to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. A Muslim visitor in Borno is exposed through the Shari'a track; other visitors are exposed through the state morality statute and its courts.
tangentialFactors:
Borno's criminalisation operates through two state enactments that sit alongside each other: the 2000 statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities, and the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001. The same conduct can be reached under either, and the 2000 statute assigns cases across Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts rather than to a single forum.

Section 4 of the 2000 statute deems all brothels closed on commencement, removing a category of premises in the state. Section 3 also reaches prostitution and pimping, offences that do not require same-sex conduct.
localsOnly:
For residents of Borno, the 2000 statute's offence list extends beyond same-sex conduct to prostitution, pimping and the keeping of brothels, and Section 4 closed all brothels in the state from commencement. The Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 adds a separate state-level Shari'a layer, signed into law on 3 March 2003.

The hisbah morality police operate in the northern Shari'a states. The UK Home Office note covers enforcement of the Shari'a provisions and the hisbah's posture, and Borno is one of the twelve states where those provisions apply to Muslims.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Borno-specific enforcement record appears in the sources: no arrests, prosecutions, convictions or trans-specific violence incidents in the state are documented. Whether Borno's death-penalty provision has ever been applied is not established by the available material.

The sourcebook that records Borno's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 identifies no operation date or gazette for it, and the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed; Borno is consequently not among the individually annotated Sharia penal codes. The commencement of that layer is unresolved.

The sources hold no Borno-specific material on health-care access, identity documents, entry and visa practice, or screening at ports of entry.
